Amber heat health alerts have been issued for much of eastern England for later this week as temperatures rise again.
The East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under the amber alerts from 9am on Wednesday until 9am Thursday.
With the temperature forecast to peak in the mid-30s Celsius on Wednesday, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), which issues the alerts, warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.
Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands, and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.
This latest heatwave comes after some of the driest regions of the UK missed their chance of rain over the weekend.
Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall on Saturday and Sunday, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.
But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.
It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.
The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 34-35C (93-95F) in south-east England or the East of England.
How hot will it get this week?
The hot weather will initially be focused on central and eastern England by Tuesday before spreading slightly northwards and westwards into midweek.
However, Wednesday is likely to be the hottest day, with readings of 30-35C across the Midlands, southern and eastern England.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will generally remain cooler and showery with temperatures in the high teens or low to mid-20s Celsius.
Current forecasts suggest that the intense heat across southern and central areas of the UK this week will be short-lived compared to previous heatwaves this summer.
No substantial rain on the horizon for driest regions
Over the weekend, rainfall was focused mainly across the north and west of the UK.
Meanwhile, the driest locations - including central, southern and eastern England - saw little, if any, meaningful rainfall.
As the spell of hot weather develops across England and Wales, the lack of significant rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels are likely to become an increasing concern.
The driest parts of England and Wales have seen exceptionally low rainfall so far this month.
Some areas, particularly in parts of north Wales and southern and eastern England, have recorded only a few millimetres of rain or even less.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in south-east England with 40 days of no rainfall up to and including 26 July.
In the driest spots, totals have been below 2% of the average July rainfall.

Your editorial quoting Sam Johnson-Schlee saying that our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe is under threat is not news to environmental health officers working in housing (The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed, 23 July). Every day they are faced with homes that contain threats to the health and safety of occupiers – from excess heat or cold, or damp and mould. For many years there has been a lack of resources, including environmental health staff to inspect homes or the political will to tackle the problems on the scale needed.
You are right to suggest that a new approach is required, but we can also learn from the 1970s, when local authorities would take the lead on collective action to improve housing. So councils should be the place to look to get things moving. This will require funding, not only to help homeowners but also to ensure that councils have sufficient staff with the right skills.
After the 1981 English House Condition Survey, which showed the high rate of disrepair in the housing stock, the government introduced generous repair grants, and contributed £1bn through subsidies. The decision to discontinue funding for the private sector housing renewal programme, which had been reduced to £376m in 2009‑10, was a result of austerity. Perhaps Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner need to revisit the past to learn what can be done.
Dr Stephen Battersby
Environmental health and housing consultant (retired)

JEFFERSON, LA – The National Weather Service has issued a Heat Advisory for all of Jefferson Parish through 8 p.m. today (Monday, July 27, 2026) and an Extreme Heat Watch from 11 a.m. through 8 p.m. tomorrow (Tuesday, July 28, 2026). Actual temperatures will reach the upper 90s with a heat index of up to 112 degrees today and 115 tomorrow. Additional warnings and advisories are likely to be issued through midweek.
Hot temperatures and high humidity values will occur, leading to potential heat-related illnesses. As a reminder, Jefferson Parish libraries are open and can be used for residents to get out of the heat. The Jefferson Parish Library system consists of 17 locations that stretch from the Lakeshore Branch on the edge of Lake Pontchartrain to the Grand Isle Branch just steps away from the Gulf of Mexico. For library locations and hours, visit www.JPLibrary.net. Residents in need of assistance can contact the Jefferson Parish Emergency Operations Center at (504) 349-5360.
Consecutive days of dangerous heat can take a serious toll on a person’s body. The public should remain weather aware and take precautionary measures to avoid becoming a victim of heat exhaustion and related illnesses. Heat-related illnesses, like heat exhaustion or heat stroke, happen when the body is not able to properly cool itself. While the body normally cools itself by sweating, during extreme heat, this might not be enough. In these cases, a person’s body temperature rises faster than it can cool itself down. This can cause damage to the brain and other vital organs. Some factors that might increase your risk of developing a heat-related illness include high levels of humidity, obesity, fever, dehydration, prescription drug use, heart disease, mental illness, poor circulation, sunburn and alcohol use.
Heat-related illnesses and deaths are preventable:
- Wear lightweight, light-colored, loose-fitting clothing
- Stay indoors in air conditioning and limiting outdoor activities
- Look before you lock your car. The fastest heating rate inside a car occurs in the first 30 minutes. Never leave people or pets alone in a closed car.
During high temperatures, it is important to monitor those at high risk, including infants and young children, people 65 or older, those who are overweight, people who overexert during work or exercise and people who are physically ill (especially with heart disease or high blood pressure), or who take certain medications, such as for depression, insomnia or poor circulation.
It is also important to protect your four-legged friends during hot weather months. Jefferson Protection & Animal Welfare Services recommends the following:
- Animals’ paws are just as tender as your feet, so please check the pavement with your hand; if it’s too hot for you, it’s too hot for them. Pet shoes or booties help keep their paws safe.
- Even though you and your pets need exercise, it is important to avoid going out during the hottest part of the day.
- Much like humans, animals can also get sunburned; monitor your pet for burns (short and light-colored fur). Apply animal-safe sunblock, if necessary.
- A pet’s fur may actually help keep them cool in the hotter months, so reconsider before cutting off all their fur, but keep them properly groomed.
- Some pets may be more susceptible to heat (Bulldogs, Pugs, etc.); monitor these breeds for breathing issues.
- Bring water when going on a long walk, even in the earliest or latest part of the day.
- DO NOT leave your pet in a hot vehicle.
For more information about Jefferson Parish, visit www.JeffParish.gov. Residents can also receive regular updates by following the Parish on social media (@JeffParishGov) or by texting JPALERT (for English) or JPNOTICIAS (for Spanish) to 888-777.

Hot, humid weather is returning to central Indiana, with a heat advisory going into effect at 11 a.m. on Monday, July 27.
Hoosiers can expect to see temperature highs in the low 90s and heat index values of up to 110, according to the National Weather Service. The heat advisory will remain in effect until 9 p.m.

Things to remember to stay safe in the heat
The City of Indianapolis previously shared the following tips for heat safety:
- Find public cooling centers. Public buildings, such as Indy Parks family centers and Indianapolis Public Library branches, will be open across the city during normal business hours to help residents stay cool.
- Stay hydrated. Drink plenty of water.
- Check on relatives and neighbors, especially the elderly and those without access to air conditioning.

- When working outside, wear light, loose-fitting clothing. Take frequent breaks in the shade or an air-conditioned room.

- Bring pets indoors and ensure they have plenty of water to drink. Residents are reminded that city ordinance states pets are not to be outside unsupervised when the temperature is over 90 degrees or a heat advisory is in effect.

Nashville doctor shares heat exhaustion warning as temperatures soar
A Nashville doctor who helps safeguard music lovers during steamy summer festivals shared key tips on avoiding heat exhaustion at events and elsewhere to safeguard kids, adults and pets.
With Nashville-area temperatures expected to stay in the 90s for much of the final week of July, knowing how to recognize and treat heat exhaustion and heat stroke could be critical, said Dr. Ashley Panas, chief flight physician with Vanderbilt University Medical Center's LifeFlight. Panas has helped staff medical services during racing events at Nashville Superspeedway, CMA Fest and events at Nissan Stadium that bring crowds, fun and, often, heat-related illness.
"We certainly see a lot of heat-related illness," Panas said. "Early illnesses can be fairly minor but can also be fairly extreme. Heat stroke is life threatening and that's when your body core temperature starts to affect your vital organs."
Young children and the elderly are at higher risk, but healthy young adults also can become sick from the heat, she said.
Heat exhaustion symptoms include heavy sweating; headache; dizziness; fatigue; nausea or vomiting; rapid heart rate and intense thirst. Meanwhile, heat stroke comes with a body temperature of 103 degrees or higher; confusion or disorientation; slurred speech; hot, red skin and fainting, seizures or loss of consciousness.
"All ages are susceptible to heat stroke," especially when exercising in the heat, she said.
A few simple steps can keep the good times going and lessen the risks of injury.
What to do before an outdoor concert or event
Start early by drinking plenty of water the day before you plan to be outside in the heat so your body is hydrated, the doctor said.
Otherwise, if you start out dehydrated, you're going to be more susceptible of heat illness at the event.
Staying safe at Nashville festivals
Panas advised that workers and concertgoers make a mental note of the location of the medical tent as they enter the event just in case.
It's important to drink lots of water and beverages with electrolytes, she said.
Some venues will offer cooling stations with shade and water.
If alcohol is consumed, it's important to drink moderately because it can be a double-whammy, causing someone to become dehydrated more quickly and dulling the awareness of possible heat exhaustion, the doctor said.
Signs of possible heat exhaustion
If someone starts talking nonsensically, it could be a sign of heat exhaustion, Panas said. Other signs can include headaches, nausea. muscle cramping and lightheadedness.
Someone in danger of overheating may turn red or may become pale an clammy, Panas said.
Someone suffering a heat stroke might suffer a seizure or lose consciousness.
Rapid cooling
Medical teams at outdoor events have rapid cooling plans to aid victims on site before transporting them to a hospital.
"The literature in recent years has shown that if we can rapidly cool someone at the time that we identify them as a heat stroke victim, their outcomes are much better," Panas said.
The teams will move the patient to the shade and immerse them in an ice bath to lower their core temperature on site, the doctor said.
How long can you leave your pet in a hot car?
Panas advises not to leave your pet in a hot car, even with windows cracked.
Temperatures inside the car can rise quickly, endangering pets and children, according to warnings by the state Health Department.
Health experts urge drivers to routinely check front and back seats for kids and pets before leaving the car.

Heavy Rain Lashes Odisha As Deep Depression Nears Landfall, IMD Issues Red Alert For Three Districts
Revenue Minister Suresh Pujari has urged residents not to panic, assuring that state has put all machinery on high alert, reports Minati Singha.
Bhubaneswar: A deep depression over the northwest Bay of Bengal brought heavy showers across Odisha during the past 24 hours on Monday with Banki in Cuttack district recording the state's highest rainfall of 192 mm.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned that heavy rainfall is likely to intensify further, issuing a red warning for Sundargarh, Keonjhar and Mayurbhanj districts. Odisha government said the state machinery is ready for any major rainfall.
Reviewing the rain situation in different districts, Revenue Minister Suresh Pujari said, "We are ready to combat more rainfall and have put all machinery on high alert for any kind of situation. Line departments have also been alerted. Rivers are flowing well below the danger mark." He urged people not to panic and to take care of elders and children during the rains.
In the wake of the heavy rainfall forecast, four districts namely Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapada, Mayurbhanj and Subarnpur have declared holiday at educational institutes on Monday. The Special Relief Commissioner (SRC) has also issued flash flood alerts in several districts till Tuesday evening. Some districts like Cuttack, Bhadrak and Balasore have reported flash flood-like situations.
According to the IMD's midday weather bulletin, the deep depression remained centred over the northwest Bay of Bengal near the West Bengal–north Odisha coast on Monday morning and is expected to move north-northwestwards before crossing the coast between Balasore and Canning later in the day.
Director of IMD's Bhubaneswar regional centre Manorama Mohanty said, "Odisha has received 600.4 mm seasonal rainfall from June 1 to July 27 this year, which is 20 percent more than normal rainfall. The southwest monsoon remained active over Odisha, triggering moderate rain at most places and heavy to very heavy rainfall in several districts."
Among the major rainfall stations, Athagarh received 174 mm, Sonepur 135 mm, Kendrapada 133 mm, Khairmal 108 mm, Jatni 97 mm, Rajnagar 96 mm, while Mundali and Satyabadi recorded 78.2 mm and 78 mm, respectively. The state's average rainfall during the last 24 hours stood at 20.9 mm, which is 66 per cent above the normal of 12.6 mm. The district-wise rainfall map showed very heavy rainfall at four stations and heavy rainfall at 14 stations across the state.
The IMD has issued a red warning for Sundargarh, Keonjhar and Mayurbhanj, forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall at a few places with isolated extremely heavy rainfall. An orange warning has been sounded for all coastal and interior districts for the next 24 hours. Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds of 50–60 kmph are also expected over several northern and coastal districts.
The IMD cautioned that intense rainfall may lead to urban flooding, waterlogging, traffic disruptions, damage to kutcha roads and vulnerable structures, landslides in susceptible areas, and inundation of standing crops. People have been advised to avoid waterlogged areas, remain indoors during thunderstorms, and follow official weather advisories.
For Bhubaneswar, the forecast indicates a generally cloudy sky with one or two spells of rain or thundershower over the next 24 hours, with temperatures likely to hover around 32 degree Celsius and 24 degree Celsius. The city recorded 32.8 mm rainfall till 8:30 am on Monday.
Meanwhile, the IMD has advised fishermen not to venture into the sea along and off the Odisha coast till July 29, warning of squally weather with wind speeds of 40–50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph, and rough to very rough sea conditions.
